policy_title: Reform Child Benefit Household Income Threshold
stated: The Conservative Party will end the unfairness in Child Benefit by moving to a household system, so families don't start losing Child Benefit until their combined income reaches £120,000, benefitting over 700,000 households.

source.quote: End the unfairness in Child Benefit by moving to a household system, so families don’t start losing Child Benefit until their combined income reaches £120,000 – saving the average family which benefits £1,500.

bearing_set.reason: Raising the Child Benefit withdrawal threshold to £120,000 household income directly increases real disposable income for 700,000+ families currently losing the benefit, a material cash-transfer effect on household finances.

The current per-individual threshold creates a high effective marginal tax rate and a known work-disincentive for second earners in single-high-earner households; switching to a household basis materially changes those in-work incentive structures.

Raising the household income threshold to £120,000 before Child Benefit is withdrawn directly increases take-home income for the ~700,000 affected families, reducing their effective tax burden via the High Income Child Benefit Charge.
Extending Child Benefit entitlement to higher-income households reduces exchequer receipts from the HICBC without a stated offsetting revenue source, materially worsening the funded/borrowed balance.

The gains accrue exclusively to households with combined incomes between roughly £50,000 and £120,000 — well above the UK median — while lower-income families are unaffected, mechanistically widening the income gap between the top and the rest.

membership_note: A household income threshold reform to Child Benefit operates primarily as a tax-burden change (O11), with a clear fiscal cost (O12) and a regressive distributional effect (O14); cost-of-living effects for lower-income households are absent since those families are not affected.
